ENGLISH PASSAGE 3: A Library on Two Wheels

[2] A series of early sketches [[were]] pinned beside photographs of three apartment courtyards beyond the nearest branch, giving the work a visible history. Visitors could follow the sequence from initial assumption to later revision, and several left written questions that the group discussed at the next session. [3] Using weatherproof bins and a weekly request card, [[the first set of observations was recorded by the team]] before any permanent change was made. [4] The procedure initially seemed straightforward. [[However]] mystery novels circulated quickly, but picture books generated the most repeat visits. Rather than treat that detail as a nuisance, the group compared it with the earlier records and checked whether the same pattern appeared under a second set of conditions. [5] When the team discussed the evidence with visitors, [[they]] asked questions that revealed which parts of the explanation remained unclear. [6] The group could have ignored the complication [[it instead treated the problem as useful evidence]]. That decision slowed the schedule by several days, but it also produced a clearer record of why one approach had been rejected and another adopted. [7] That choice was [[completely essential and absolutely necessary]] because the original route climbed a steep avenue while the bins were full. [8] The records were especially [[nice]]: they showed why the librarians reversed the loop and scheduled the climb after most returns. The team also saved measurements from the unsuccessful version, since those values might help another group recognize the same limitation sooner.
